    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Keep reading for the latest news in Russia's war in Ukraine on Wednesday, November 25:.

    In an interview with the German MD Meets Podcast, US envoy Jared Kushner warned against a downward spiral in the conflict in Ukraine, which he described as "a proxy war where Europe is funding and arming Ukraine against Russia.".

    Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law and chosen intermediary in negotiations with Russia's Vladimir Putin, also warned that "it won't take a lot of miscalculation for this thing to escalate massively.".

    After several failed rounds of talks involving his fellow envoy, Steve Witkoff, Kushner admitted that the glitch of territoriy in eastern Ukraine remained a sticking point.

    "What Steve and I have deciphered from having many, many hours with President Putin and from the Russian team, is that you know the territorial matter is right now a little bit of a deadlock," he noted.

    However, Kushner also appeared to accuse the Europeans of hypocrisy for supporting Ukraine while continuing to spend vast sums of money on Russian energy.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    A German-Ukrainian woman accused of spying for Russia goes on trial in Berlin on Thursday.

    She is charged with providing an employee and secret agent at the Russian Embassy in Berlin with sensitive information.

    The alleged spy is accused of tipping the man off about high intelligence-value events over a period of years and helping him to secure entry.

    The dpa news agency reports that the Russian agent in question was the country's deputy military attache, who has since been expelled from Germany.

    The woman had long been known as a pro-Russian networker in the Berlin area, having lived in the country for several decades.

    The lawsuit against her from the federal prosecutor's office based in Karslruhe also alleges that she tried to "win over individuals from the Federal Defense Ministry and the weapons industry for her purposes.".

    Sources indicate that she is accused of acting out of personal conviction, rather than, say, fear or blackmail. She was arrested in January this year.

    The woman is accused of making contact with the Russian espionage asset as of October 2023 at the latest. Her most pressing task was to seek out information pertaining to Germany defense policy and the weapons industry, particularly in light of and where relevant to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

    The Ukrainian General Staff announced that Ukrainian forces had attacked a major Russian military air base, damaging five aircraft used to launch missiles and bombs at Ukraine.

    According to the General Staff, three MiG-31 jets, which are used to fire hypersonic missiles, and two Su-34 fighter-bombers were knocked out of operation "for some time.".

    The report stated that the Savasleyka air base, located east of Moscow in the Nizhny Novgorod region, had been hit in the latest long-range attacks aimed at crippling Moscow's war effort.

    Russia did not immediately comment on the announcement.

    Numerous sources inside Russian foreign policy circles on Wednesday underscored the Kremlin's desire for European diplomats to travel to Moscow and explain their intentions before they be allowed to participate in any Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations.

    Russian President Vladimir Putin originally extended the invitation last month. On Wednesday, Foreign Policy Advisor Yury Ushakov said the invitation stands but that no Europeans have so far agreed to embark on the diplomatic sojourn.

    Russia's Ambassador to Germany Sergei Nechayev on Wednesday told France's AFP news agency that reaction to Putin's invitation has been "restrained.".

    Nechayev claimed that Moscow remains, "ready to continue the dialogue and carry on with negotiations.".

    He also repeated the Kremlin claim that it is Europe that is the impediment to stopping the war, and that Russia — which launched and continues to execute its unprovoked years-long war of aggression in Ukraine — is the only party truly interested in peace.

    Nechayev remarked the Kremlin doesn't see the same "honesty" from the Europeans that it does from US President Donald Trump's team — made up of his son-in-law Jared Kushner and his friend Steve Witkoff — and wants to "know precisely what their intentions are.".

    According to recent reports, russia has been accused of foot dragging as a way to prolong attacks on Ukraine. On Wednesday, Nechayev continued in that vein, saying: "Our request to Europe is this: Decide what it is you want, determine whom you will appoint as negotiators, and, most importantly, clarify what you aim to achieve.".

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Poland's Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk told reporters that Warsaw will set up a no-fly zone inside its border with Ukraine and suggested other regional allies do the same in the wake of repeated Russian incursions into NATO airspace as part of Moscow's war of aggression.

    "An ordinance is already being prepared by the government and should enter into force at the end of December or the beginning of January," said Tomczyk.

    "We will also urge our allies — the ⁠entire ​NATO alliance — to establish such a ​principle along the eastern flank," he continued, "Poland was a pioneer ​in this regard, ‌and the Baltic states have since followed our lead.".

    Poland strictly limits air traffic at its border already.

    On Wednesday, Tomczyk noted the proposed no-fly zone will cover several dozen kilometers of territory from the border and provide added support for Poland's armed forces.

    German Chancellor Friedrich Merz defended his government's expenditures on Ukraine aid during a budget debate in the Bundestag on Wednesday.

    Merz tackled criticism from opposition parties on the left and right head on, saying "Russia knows exactly ​what it wants. And Russia wants more than Ukraine.".

    According to recent reports, "Russia is escalating in the Baltic region, in Poland, on the Black Sea. Russia ​is escalating ‌in space. And Russia is now escalating massively here, in our own country, too, even at the risk of loss of life," he added.

    Merz said, "anyone who doesn't see that, doesn't understand the world around them, or they are pursuing entirely different aims.".

    The Left Party and Alternative for Germany (AfD) have both called for an end to Ukraine aid and better relations with Moscow.

    Among other things, Germany blames Russia for an explosive drone incident at Leipzig airport this summer as well as cyberattacks, sabotage and airspace incursions across the EU and NATO.

    In a recent development, merz said on Wednesday that by supporting Ukraine, Germany is protecting itself. "We are learning from Ukraine," said Merz, "technologically for civilian use but of course also in defense ⁠technology.".

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Kyiv and Moscow both assessed damage to energy infrastructure on Wednesday morning as both sides continued to inflict damage on one another amid Russia's over four-and-a-half-year attempted invasion of neighboring Ukraine.

    Russia again focused its attacks on Ukraine's energy structure in an attempt to break the will of the country's civilian population as the bitter cold of winter sets in.

    Moscow's troops attacked a thermal energy power plant, shutting it down; as well as targeting a gas production facility in Poltawa, where ensuing fires also shut down operations.

    Ukraine's acting energy minister said that power outages were reported in five regions as a result of the Russian attacks.

    In Russia's Samara region, Ukrainian drones hit at least two oil refineries, killing one person, sparking large fires and and causing energy blackouts.

    Kyiv's attacks on Russian ships in and off the coast of Libya over the past couple of days have ruffled feathers among Ukraine's allies, with France and Italy, for instance, coming down on entirely different sides of the concern.

    French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot noted Kyiv was justified in its actions because it has an "absolute right to self-defense." Libya on Wednesday unveiled that two of its soldiers had died from injuries sustained during a weekend drone attack that sank a Russian warship.

    Speaking with French broadcaster TF1, Barrot noted, "For nearly five years now, [Russian President] Vladimir Putin has not only been bombing Ukraine, but has also been constantly engaging in acts of aggression and harassing Europeans in an attempt to undermine our unity.".

    Barrot stated Russia alone is to blame for the war and its expansion, and then asked, "What would we do if we were being bombarded day and night by an enemy — an invader?".

    Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani on Wednesday criticized Kyiv's actions, saying, "It was a mistake to violate Libya's sovereignty" and warned against further similar activities in other regions.

    Speaking with Italy's Corriere della Sera newspaper ‌on ⁠Wednesday, Tajani remarked, "Italy was absolutely unaware of Kyiv's intentions to strike in ​Libyan territorial waters, even inside a port.".

    Tajani said he had spoken with Ukraine Foreign Minister Andrii Sybihato and conveyed Italy's concern over the matter, adding that Rome would continue its staunch support for Ukraine and its sovereignty while at the same time seeking to keep the conflict from spreading.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    As Russia's invasion of Ukraine creeps toward its fifth year, both sides continue to blast each other's infrastructure.

    Overnight attacks targeted gas, oil and thermal energy facilities on both sides of the conflict's front lines.

    While Moscow chided former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson's calls for a contingent of Western soldiers to be stationed in Ukraine, France's foreign minister defended Kyiv's recent attacks on Russian maritime vessels in far away Libya — something Italy's foreign minister criticized.

    In Berlin, Chancellor Friedrich Merz defended German support for Ukraine as opposition parties with sympathies for Moscow complain it's too expensive.

    Merz called out those wanting to curtail support as either "failing to grasp" the fact that "Russia wants more than Ukraine" or "pursuing entirely different aims with regard to our country's freedom, openness and liberalism.".

    Lastly, Poland's defense minister on Wednesday expressed astonishment over the fact that the US has not yet condemned or even reacted to repeated Russian drone and missile incursions into Polish airspace in recent days.

    • On Wednesday, Flipkart said it would announce Krishnamurthy’s successor in the coming weeks, and Chief Product and Technology Officer Balaji Thiagarajan will lead the manufacturer until a replacement is found.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Kalyan Krishnamurthy (pictured above), who steered Flipkart through Walmart’s acquisition in 2018 and helped build it into one of India’s biggest e-commerce companies, is stepping down as chief executive next week after more than 11 years with the company.

    On Wednesday, Flipkart said it would announce Krishnamurthy’s successor in the coming weeks, and Chief Product and Technology Officer Balaji Thiagarajan will lead the manufacturer until a replacement is found.

    A Walmart spokesperson told TechCrunch that Krishnamurthy’s last day at Flipkart will be December 4.

    Krishnamurthy joined Flipkart in 2015 from Tiger Global, one of the company’s early investors, and became its CEO in 2017. He remained at the helm after Walmart acquired a controlling stake in the company for $16 billion in 2018.

    Sources indicate that under Krishnamurthy, Flipkart said its business grew more than five-fold. The firm has more than 500 million registered users and over 1.4 million sellers, including those on Shopsy, its low-cost shopping platform. The company’s marketplace offers over 150 million products across more than 80 categories.

    In a recent development, flipkart has of late moved into newer segments, including quick-commerce through Flipkart Minutes and, more recently, food delivery through a venture called Eat-in by Minutes. The expansion is targeted at Indian consumers who are increasingly turning to quick-delivery services for everything from groceries to electronics.

    According to recent reports, thiagarajan joined Flipkart in September last year to lead its product and technology teams. Before that, he had founded Kasu.ai, a Bay Area startup working on AI assistants for corporate finance. He also previously worked at Google, Microsoft, and Uber in senior engineering positions, per his LinkedIn profile.

    Recent findings suggest that krishnamurthy’s exit comes amid uncertainty around Flipkart’s IPO. In March, the tech giant moved its headquarters from Singapore to India as part of its preparations to go public, but in May, Walmart reportedly told Flipkart to delay its IPO and focus on becoming profitable first.

    Walmart declined to comment beyond its announcement when asked what prompted Krishnamurthy’s departure, and whether the leadership change would affect Flipkart’s IPO aims. Flipkart did not respond to a request for comment.

    Sources indicate that founded in 2007 by Sachin and Binny Bansal as an online bookstore, much like its bigger rival Amazon, Flipkart eventually expanded into other categories. Under Krishnamurthy, it has grown into India’s largest online retailer by gross merchandise value, ahead of Amazon.

    It has been revealed that “Both Flipkart and Walmart are better because of Kalyan. We are grateful for his leadership, the governance he instilled and his many contributions to the organization,” Chris Nicholas, president and CEO, Walmart International, mentioned in a statement.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A Russian MiG-31 military jet (file photo).

    Ukraine has noted it damaged five Russian military aircraft in an attack on Russia's Savasleyka airfield, 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow.

    It has been revealed that three MiG-31 and two Su-34s aircraft were hit, Kyiv's General Staff said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed but that "there may be even better news to come". It did not elaborate on what weapons it had used to hit the airfield.

    Russia has not commented on the strikes.

    It has been revealed that the airfield at Savasleyka, in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, has been a target for Ukraine for several years. It hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs.

    The take-off of MiG-31s in particular frequently triggers nationwide alerts across Ukraine, as the Kinzhal missiles they carry have been known to hit large infrastructure and military targets and are difficult to shoot down.

    Overnight, Kyiv also stated it hit two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region some 800km (500 miles) from the front line â the latest in a series of long-range strikes which have dented Moscow's oil processing capacity.

    "Did you repair them? We'll hit them again," the defence ministry in Kyiv said.

    Sources indicate that samara region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said the night-time attacks had been "a true ordeal", with more than 145 drones shot down. One person was killed and several towns experienced power outages, Fedorishchev said.

    Kyiv also said it had hit a radar system as well as fuel and logistics depots across Ukrainian territories currently occupied by Russia.

    "Without fuel, military vehicles cannot move; without ammunition, artillery falls silent," the defence ministry stated, adding that every successful hit meant Moscow could carry out fewer strikes.

    Kyiv has developed a thriving weapons industry and Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets well beyond the front line have become commonplace in the years since Moscow debuted its full-scale invasion.

    On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin called for a tightening of security measures across the country's energy facilities.

    But he also argued that Russia had managed to stabilise its domestic fuel market without suffering "critical damage" and added that Moscow would "inevitably" retaliate against Kyiv.

    It has been revealed that ukraine continues to come under daily attack. Ten people were killed across several regions between 24 and 25 November, while thousands are without power after Russian strikes on energy infrastructure.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse. The two tech giants are reportedly discussing a potential deal that would allow Meta’s popular AI agent to connect directly to Amazon’s store.

    The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out.

    According to a Wednesday report by Fortune, citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter. Two key challenges remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement.

    It has been revealed that one of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business. In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.

    Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace. If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers.

    Fortune reported that executives are concerned that third-party shopping agents could weaken Amazon’s direct relationship with consumers, according to people familiar with the matter.

    Any potential agreement between Amazon and Meta would reportedly require approval from both companies’ CEOs, Fortune also reported.

    Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers.
    • In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:.
    • Sources indicate that we see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers. To examine what such attacks on data centers mean for the future of cloud services that all modern societies depend upon, Ars hosted a live discussion.

    In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:.

    Sources indicate that we see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well. The dual use that I refer to is the utilization of compute functions within these data centers—within cloud services—by militaries, for example, to run battlefield management systems, to do their HR, to do their resource management. Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there’s an incentive to target it.

    Jarnecki also highlighted the fact that relatively cheap kamikaze drones can inflict disproportionate economic costs and create widespread cloud disruptions when striking data centers:.

    Sources indicate that the second reason that we’ve seen targeting particularly in Russia’s largest data centers or some of Russia’s largest public cloud data centers like Yandex, as well as American hyperscalers that are based in the Gulf, is to impose economic cost in a way that would be disadvantageous for an adversary and would otherwise be quite difficult to impose in other ways. So it’s relatively low cost of munition to high cost of disruption. If you think about the amount of investment that’s been put forward by AWS and other companies in the Gulf to build out these data center installations relative to the cost of the amount of Shahed drones that are manufactured, produced, and utilized by Iran to target these data centers, I would put it very, very conservatively at 100X or even more. The cost ratio is really very lucrative for the adversary, and it provides the opportunity to really degrade the economic outcomes of who you are targeting.

    According to recent reports, much of the discussion also focused on cloud resilience lessons for both governments and hyperscalers, with the latter including large cloud and data center operators such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta. Jarnecki highlighted the example of how Ukraine took steps to safeguard its cloud infrastructure when Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered Russian military forces to launch the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022:.

    I think that Ukraine anticipated this problem set very effectively. They anticipated and understood that Russia would not be discriminating necessarily in its targeting of civilian digital infrastructure particularly, and therefore conducted a large-scale cloud migration at the onset of the full-scale war in part in reaction to the anticipated targeting but then also actual targeting that took place through kinetic means.

    Such lessons are vital because 2026 is unlikely to be the last year in which data centers come under substantial military attack, Jarnecki mentioned:.

    Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, I think that this really does indicate a continuation of this kind of targeting, not just because data centers are, despite efforts to harden some of them, relatively squishy, relatively easy to find, and have the potential, because of their complexity, to induce cascading risks within the facility or more widely if they are hit particularly by kinetic munitions. So at present, I would say it’s a dangerous trend that is likely to crop up again.

    Throughout the event, Jarnecki also addressed viewer questions about whether data centers can realistically be hardened or built underground to withstand physical attacks, and even how orbital data centers or low-Earth orbit satellite constellations such as Starlink could provide backup options from space.

    Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (911 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis.
    • The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).
    • Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

    The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

    Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

    It has been revealed that the development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, remarked the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.

    To this end, he unveiled the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.

    Industry observers note that however, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the 2023 election, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

    These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of upcoming proportions.

    Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace.".

    "This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," noted Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.

    "We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.

    Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing.".

    According to recent reports, he added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.

    "Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," mentioned Mgbeahuruike.

    Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, the director-general of state-owned broadcaster Voice of Nigeria, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

    He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.

    Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

    Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

    Ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the fresh standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

    However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.

    Industry observers note that voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth. The 2023 election recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27% of registered voters going to the polls.

    An Israeli air strike in the Gaza Strip has killed a senior Hamas security official and three members of his family, according to local doctors and the Hamas-run interior ministry.

    Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters died when their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City was bombed at dawn, the ministry stated.

    The Israeli military noted Abu al-Ouf was a "terrorist" and that he was eliminated "to remove the threat he posed".

    On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.

    Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza.

    Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam states.

    Wednesday's strike in Shati caused extensive damage to the Abu al-Ouf family's apartment.

    Photos showed the exterior wall and several interior walls were destroyed, with rubble and broken furniture left scattered across the floor.

    An interior ministry statement said that Abu al-Ouf was killed along with his wife Noura, 41, and their daughters Yusra, 15, and Jana, 13.

    It condemned the attack as a "heinous crime" and accused Israel of targeting security personnel in Gaza "in an effort to spread chaos within Palestinian society".

    Hamas's internal security service is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting the group's infrastructure and rooting out informants.

    Israel's military mentioned in a statement that Abu al-Ouf was a "significant figure" who had served as "a key source of expertise" in efforts to restrict Israeli counter-terrorism operations in Gaza.

    "His elimination is a blow to the apparatus's leadership capabilities and follows yesterday's elimination of his commander," it added.

    On Tuesday, an Israeli drone strike in western Gaza City killed Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service.

    He had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid in Gaza City by Israeli special forces.

    Near daily Israeli strikes continue in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreed in October last year.

    At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

    Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.

    The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

    Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry notes.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The feature is now rolling out in public beta.

    WhatsApp's latest public beta release adds a fresh feature that could make chatting with your friends more fun: stickers that play sounds when you tap them. You know how the chat app lets you create your own stickers, even animated ones? Well, it's pretty much the same thing, except you can also add audio. That gives you an easy way to recreate iconic video clips, such as Josh Hutcherson's Whistle edit meme, which has been making the rounds again thanks to the Sunrise on the Reaping movie.

    According to WABetaInfo, sound stickers are part of beta patch 2.26.41.3 for Android. If you want to try it out, you can apply to become a tester for the chat app through Google Play. To make a sound sticker, open a chat, tap the sticker icon and then tap Create sticker. From there, you can choose a video from your library, which WhatsApp will automatically convert into a sticker.

    It has been revealed that now, you'll find the fresh Sound icon at the top menu. Tap it to open the new Add sound screen. From there, you can keep the video's original audio, record a voice note or any other custom sound you want to use, or choose an audio file saved on your phone. When you're done, you can save the sound sticker and send it to as many people as you want.

    Since the feature is experimental, you might not be able to access it right now, even if you're already a beta tester. WhatsApp has yet to announce whether it will roll out to all customers in the future.

    Latest Update: Todoist confirms 6% of customers’ details were stolen in data breach

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Task management app Todoist said on Tuesday that a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates.
    • According to recent reports, todoist mentioned the attacker used stolen credentials to access the company’s version control system and source code between November 22 and 23.
    • It has been revealed that the hacker downloaded credentials of early Todoist consumers whose passwords were stored using an older hashing method, but didn’t change any source code, the organization noted.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Task management app Todoist said on Tuesday that a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates. The organization said around 6% of its customers were affected and blamed stolen credentials for the breach.

    According to recent reports, todoist mentioned the attacker used stolen credentials to access the company’s version control system and source code between November 22 and 23. The hacker then changed employee access controls and reached the app’s cloud infrastructure via an employee’s work account.

    It has been revealed that the hacker downloaded credentials of early Todoist consumers whose passwords were stored using an older hashing method, but didn’t change any source code, the organization noted. Todoist said it has blocked the attack path and reset passwords as a mitigation step, as well as disabled the Todoist for Outlook email add-on.

    For a small number of people, about 0.001% of its userbase, the hacker also searched through tasks, comments, and attachment names to look for credentials for other services, like API keys and access tokens.

    The hacker also pulled Todoist API tokens and Slack integration tokens, and looked for emails, addresses, and attachment file names through the Todoist for Outlook extension if it was connected to accounts and had permission to read emails.

    The firm said it has sent a notice to those affected and asked them to reset their credentials and change their login details in other places with the same password. The company is asking users to also patch API tokens, reconnect integrations, and revoke or replace any access keys, recovery phrases, or credentials they had stored in Todoist comments.

    Todoist remarked it has also reset its internal access structure and how remote command execution works in its cloud environment to prevent such incidents in the future.

    Todoist’s founder and CEO Amir Salihefendić apologized to people about the incident on X, and mentioned the company will take a closer look at why it happened.

    The to-do app’s data breach is the latest in a burgeoning list of data breaches in which hackers use stolen credentials to access data and systems at enterprises. So far this year, we’ve seen several companies fall victim to this form of attack, including Uber and Klue.

The discussions, which could end Amazon’s block on Muse, reportedly center on the kinds of products the AI agent recommends and the potential impact on the ecommerce giant’s advertising revenue.

Neither Amazon nor Meta immediately responded to The Verge’s request for comment.

    Though some online retailers, such as Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, and Sephora, have opened their digital doors to AI agents like Muse, Amazon has been more hesitant. Amazon also blocked Perplexity’s AI agent from shopping on its site, and has instead focused on promoting its own Alexa for Shopping assistant, which customers can now text to shop on their behalf.

    • After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s new AI policies, which appeared to allow the organization to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance.
    • In a note published on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the tech giant’s terms of service and admitted that her team “should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content.”.
    • “Our recent terms upgrade was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we’re using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s new AI policies, which appeared to allow the organization to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance.

    In a note published on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the tech giant’s terms of service and admitted that her team “should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content.”.

    “Our recent terms upgrade was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we’re using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week. “It was not meant to enable us to train AI models for the purpose of creating copycats of your items. We do not and will not do that.”.

    Aaron Meshon, a longtime professional illustrator and Etsy seller, told Ars that even though the company had dialed back its AI language somewhat, the changes were mere “sugar coating.”.

    He said he still aims on shutting down his 15-year-old Etsy store on December 1.

    In a recent development, “I would say I’m losing 20 percent of my yearly income,” he stated. “It’s a few mortgage payments.”.

    He noted that Etsy’s announcement also seems to be rather tone-deaf, given that many retailers make a substantial portion of their annual revenue in the run-up to the end-of-year holiday season.

    “This is the worst two-to-three weeks out of the year to do this, bar none,” he said.

    The fracas began earlier this month, when the organization first proposed newly introduced contractual language. The updated terms read:.

    As a result, a slew of vendors pulled up stakes, with some saying they had “burned their Etsy shop to the ground” or that they “just killed our Etsy store after 13 years.”.

    Etsy’s change is reminiscent of a recent dust-up involving Meta, where the tech giant had wanted to “require Meta Business account users to allow extensive AI training on external websites linked on Facebook.” Meta then indefinitely paused that move.

    Last month, Etsy also told sellers that it would “set clearer restrictions on AI use,” despite the fact that AI-generated items remain for sale all over the site.

    “Today, many active buyers say they can’t tell which items involve AI-generated content,” James Ossman, the company’s vice president of customer operations, wrote on October 22. “It’s become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy.”.

    For years, Etsy has been notoriously poor at enforcing its own rules, not only regarding AI but also the official prohibitions on selling sex toys, pornography, and even purported witchcraft spells.

    Thanks to its Intel Arc G3 Extreme chip, you get top-notch graphics for $350 less than its closest rival.

    In a recent development, modern handheld PCs started out as complimentary devices, compact systems designed to help you game on the go when you didn't have access to your beefy setup at home. But as the category has matured, we've seen manufacturers pursue higher tiers of performance. This culminated most recently in systems like MSI's Claw 8 EX AI+, which delivers serious graphics power along with an equally serious price of $1,800. But now, Acer is trying to undercut the current framerate champ with the Predator Atlas 8, equipping it with the exact same chip used in MSI's machine, but for $350 less. The result is a compelling package that delivers on many of the same highs while easing the burden on your wallet.

    With the Predator Atlas 8, Acer hasn't strayed too far from the basic template we've seen on so many other portable PCs. The middle of the system is dominated by a large 8-inch LCD TFT display with a 120Hz refresh and respectable 500-nit brightness. On the outside you get TMR analog sticks along with an Xbox-style button layout. I must admit I'm not a huge fan of Acer's circular D-Pad as it's a bit mushy and doesn't feel super precise. But if you're not playing fighting games or similar titles, it's more than serviceable for navigating menus. And if I'm really nitpicking, colors from the Predator's TFT screen aren't quite as rich as what you get from MSI's machine, but it's the kind of difference that you only really notice when you look at the two systems side by side.

    Around back, Acer included a pair of rear paddles, two shoulder buttons and analog Hall-effect triggers with plenty of travel — the latter of which are great for racing games. Along the top edge of the system you get all of the Predator Atlas 8's ports, which includes dual USB-C jacks with support for Thunderbolt 4, a microSD card reader for expandable storage, a 3.5mm audio jack and a power button with a built-in fingerprint reader.

    It has been revealed that all told, it's a pretty standard setup, though the Predator does lack a USB-A port like you get on the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. I also noticed that while Acer's dual two-watt speakers can get surprisingly loud, audio becomes distorted at higher volumes (above 50 TK) that results in a crackly or crunchy sound. That remarked, the speakers are so punchy, I found that I never really needed to turn them up that high. Unless you're trying to DJ a house party with this thing, you might not even notice.

    In a recent development, the real star of the Atlas 8 is its Intel Arc G3 Extreme processor, which is the exact same chip used in the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. The main difference is that Acer's handheld comes with 512GB of storage instead of 1TB and tops out with 24GB of shared memory (compared to 32GB on the MSI). This discrepancy almost entirely accounts for the price gap between the two systems. But for people striving for top-notch performance while trying to save a few bucks, the framerate delta in games isn't as pronounced as you might think.

    When I tested this out in Cyberpunk 2077 at 35 watts on FHD, medium graphics and XeSS set to performance, the Predator Atlas 8 hit 88 fps, which is barely more than five percent lower than the 95 fps I got from the Claw 8 EX AI+. But it's notable to note that this was using Acer's highest performance mode. When I set the system to 15 watts (which you might do when playing on battery only), the Predator and the Claw were essentially dead even in Returnal at FHD and medium graphics (60 fps for the Acer vs 59 fps for the MSI). This means that if you're trying to decide between the two, you really need to consider how you blueprint on using your handheld and what types of games you'll be playing.

    Sources indicate that similar to other high-end Windows handhelds, the Atlas 8 comes with Microsoft's Xbox experience. This software allows you to boot into a dedicated UI for gaming instead of needing to deal with the traditional desktop OS. This also makes it super easy to download all of the most popular launchers and storefronts like Epic, Steam, Battle.net and more, and because it's Windows underneath, you get better compatibility than what you get from SteamOS-powered portables. That said, if you're the type to travel with a portable monitor, keyboard and mouse, you can still switch over to the classic Windows interface to get some work done too.

    According to recent reports, the Atlas 8 is powered by an 80WHr battery that provides ample longevity, though it can vary quite a bit depending on what you're playing. However, without even doing anything to boost its longevity, I was able to play World of Warcraft: Forever at FHD on medium settings for an hour and 45 minutes on a single charge while still keeping frame rates consistently above 90. On the flipside, when I played a less demanding title like Warhammer Survivors, Acer's machine had more battery life than I knew what to do with: It lasted for more than three hours before needing to be plugged in. Notably, both of those games were played using the handheld's 30-watt Balanced performance mode, so if you're not afraid to mess around with its settings, there's a lot of room to tweak this thing to get even longer untethered gaming sessions.

    I'm still not sure how I feel about PC handhelds that cost well above $1,000. For me, that's just a ton of money to drop on a system that can't multitask as well as a similarly priced gaming laptop. However, for mobile gaming enthusiasts trying to find the sweet spot between price, performance and portability, Acer has carved out an interesting niche with the Predator Atlas 8.

    It has been revealed that at $1,450, it costs $350 less than the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, while sporting the exact same processor and delivering essentially 95 percent of the performance. That said, Acer's more approachable pricing leaves the Predator with a bit less RAM and storage, though having a microSD card slot provides a workaround for the latter. There are also some minor differences, like the lack of a USB-A port, a slightly less colorful TFT display and speakers that sound a bit wonky at high volumes. But these shortcomings could very well be a worthwhile trade-off for anyone looking for peak handheld gaming performance without completely fragging their budget.

    Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiers.
    • At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.
    • The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiers.

    At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.

    The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.

    BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.

    Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.

    Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that only Russia's defence ministry could officially report data on losses: "I suggest no other data be taken into account." The defence ministry has not released any official casualty figures for several years.

    Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.

    Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, upcoming memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.

    The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.

    Industry observers note that the data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.

    In a recent development, during the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.

    Industry observers note that russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.

    For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files.

    Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.

    Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.

    The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.

    We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.

    Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.

    According to recent reports, as this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian â unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.

    Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.

    Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.

    Sources indicate that according to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).

    In a recent development, some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.

    In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.

    At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.

    This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.

    The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.

    The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant.

    In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.

    In that 10-year war, an estimated 15,000 Red Army troops died, and an estimated one million civilians were killed.

    Additional reporting by Ilya Barabanov.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that U.S. insurer Allstate has been experiencing a tech outage since Monday morning, leaving customers nationwide unable to access their accounts, review their policy information, file claims, pay their bills, and more, just ahead of the U.S. Thanksgiving holidays.

    The outage has been impacting both the company’s website and mobile app, TechCrunch confirmed.

    Sources indicate that the breakdown follows a report from earlier this month that Allstate was planning to lay off up to 10% of its staff as part of an AI-driven efficiency push. (The manufacturer had not confirmed the report, which was attributed to unnamed sources.).

    Allstate’s outage is the latest in a series of disruptions to services such as Microsoft Outlook and Teams, the airlines, Apple Pay, and several banks. Trump administration officials have remarked the outages are not being caused by cyberattacks, but are rather being caused by a recent set of upgrades to systems, many of which run on older technology. Those systems are now in need of more frequent security and bug fixes as AI makes it easier and faster to discover vulnerabilities.

    Downdetector, a crowdsourced outage-reporting website, highlights users began reporting Allstate’s outage from Monday morning. However, the manufacturer hasn’t yet issued a formal statement about the disruption, what’s causing it, or when it may be resolved. In the meantime, local insurance agents have been fielding calls and emails from customers who aren’t able to use the company’s online services.

    According to recent reports, the timing of the outage is particularly bad given that Thanksgiving is a big travel holiday in the U.S., which means there will be car accidents. Customers will be left without a way to get in touch with their auto insurer to file claims and get roadside assistance through Allstate’s app.

    Allstate did not immediately return a request for comment.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A European Union (EU) court told the bloc on Wednesday to draw a newly introduced timeline for plans to ban cages for farm animals.
    • Judges at the European General Court ruled that the EU has failed to follow through on a pledge to ban the practice.
    • Recent findings suggest that in 2021, the European Commission set out the goal to pass a legislation by the end of 2023 to stop farmers from cooping hens, rabbits, sows and other animals in cages.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A European Union (EU) court told the bloc on Wednesday to draw a newly introduced timeline for plans to ban cages for farm animals.

    Judges at the European General Court ruled that the EU has failed to follow through on a pledge to ban the practice.

    Recent findings suggest that in 2021, the European Commission set out the goal to pass a legislation by the end of 2023 to stop farmers from cooping hens, rabbits, sows and other animals in cages. The move came after 1,4 million people signed a petition.

    It has been revealed that but it failed to follow up on the pledge. This resulted in the campaigners requesting a fresh timeline and eventually led to a court case when that was also not happening.

    The Luxembourg-based General Court, the European Union's second-highest, on Wednesday ruled in favor of the animal rights campaigners.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    "The Commission is under an obligation — which is not limited in time — to set out a timeline for all the measures which it intends to take in response to such an initiative," the court said.

    According to the "European citizens' initiative" system, the Commission has to receive the petitions that gather over one million signatures across at least seven bloc countries. However, it is not obligated to meet the demands.

    The court noted that if the Commission decides to take action, it has to keep the public and the European Parliament posted on a timeline in accordance with the principle of "good administration.".

    The Commission said it was analyzing the ruling before making a decision. It can still appeal the ruling.

    It has previously stated an intention to put forward a proposal for the phased elimination of cage systems for chickens by the end of this year, as well as a separate proposal to transition from farrowing crates to pen-based systems for pigs by 2027.

    According to the Albert Schweitzer Foundation, no timetable has been set for calves, rabbits, ducks, geese and quail.

    In the EU, about 143 million egg-laying chickens are kept in cages while the majority of female pigs spend at least part of their lives caged.

    The use of cage systems in agricultural production accredited as "organic" is already prohibited in the EU.

    #104576. My family were killed in Ukraine. My mum blamed Zelensky's troops - the truth is complicated

    My family were killed in Ukraine. My mum blamed Zelensky's troops - the truth is complicated

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2146 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Watch: BBC reporter investigates deaths of family members in Russia-Ukraine war.
    • Recent findings suggest that I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine.
    • The woman who sent me the photo states the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Watch: BBC reporter investigates deaths of family members in Russia-Ukraine war.

    Recent findings suggest that I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering.

    The woman who sent me the photo states the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse.

    The photo Anastasiya was sent of her grandparents' graves.

    I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message.

    Sources indicate that "Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it stated.

    It turned my world upside down.

    Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life.

    Recent findings suggest that mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow introduced its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict.

    Anastasiya (bottom left) with her father (top left) and grandparents (right) before the war.

    Backing Moscow is not that unusual in the Donbas region - the predominantly Russian-speaking part of eastern Ukraine where my village Dachne is located.

    After pro-Russian forces captured large parts of the Donbas in 2014, many of those who stayed supported Moscow over Kyiv, a stance cemented by exposure to Russian state TV.

    Now the Russians occupy almost 80% of Donetsk - the part of the Donbas where my village is. Over the past nearly five years, since Russia's full-scale invasion, entire towns and cities have been razed to the ground, external.

    The remains of Anastasiya's family home are circled in a frame of a video, filmed by Ukraine's 33rd Mechanised Brigade on 27 January 2025.

    I had already fallen out with my sister Sasha, who had been living in Moscow with her young family when the war broke out. She refused to take sides - I felt hurt and cut her off.

    But earlier this year, around the first anniversary of dad's death, Sasha unexpectedly texted me. We started talking over text about our childhood - the way things used to be. I realised I was not angry with her anymore. She too was grieving, missing dad just as much as I was.

    Anastasiya's father Serezha - he stayed in Dachne to look after his elderly parents.

    I told her I wanted to make a documentary about dad and she was very supportive. I knew then that I had an ally on my journey. But we decided not to tell our mum just yet.

    I started looking for witnesses to the events in Dachne that took place in January 2025, the month dad is believed to have been killed. It was not easy. It was a village of a few hundred people, but many had left, others had died, and those who remained had limited phone signals.

    Russia publicly revealed the capture of Dachne on 14 February and it has remained under Moscow's control ever since.

    Industry observers note that this meant it was impossible for me to travel there in person. So I began trying to contact my family's neighbours.

    Anastasiya could not safely travel back to Dachne, so she worked through contacts in village group chats.

    In a Dachne village messaging chat, I found the number of a man I'll call Misha. I was told he had been with my father on the day he died. Speaking to the BBC could put him in danger with the Russian occupiers, so I did not tell him I worked for the BBC or that I was recording our call.

    Misha told me that on 26 January he had looked in on my father and realised he had been injured. Serezha told him he had been "clipped" by a drone, and had asked Misha to bring a first aid kit, he said.

    It is impossible to know which side was operating the drone that killed my father, but we do know that Russian drones were constantly targeting the village at that time.

    "I asked if the wound was serious. He [Serezha] remarked it wasn't," said Misha - but then recalling how, when he had returned to check on my father a couple of hours later, he had found him dead.

    With the help of two other villagers, Misha remarked they had buried him in the greenhouse.

    "I'm sorry I couldn't save him," Misha told me.

    BBC Eye Investigations: Who Killed My Family?

    BBC journalist Anastasiya Gribanova investigates who killed her father and grandparents in Ukraine, uncovering painful accounts as she tries to reunite her divided family.

    Watch on BBC iPlayer or listen on BBC Sounds now (UK only).

    If you are outside of the UK, listen to the Who Killed My Family podcast here.

    Watch our YouTube documentary here, external.

    As for my grandparents, my investigations suggested the events surrounding their deaths may have been more complicated.

    Industry observers note that their house, on the eastern side of Dachne, had been destroyed. Neighbours told me they had escaped to another home on the same street.

    I eventually reached a woman I'll call Lina, who lived nearby and was the last person, as far as I know, who saw my grandparents alive.

    She could not recall what this date was, but knew it was in the second half of January.

    At this time, she mentioned, "the Russians were fully advancing - the edges of the village were being shelled. Then the Ukrainian soldiers moved from the edge of the village into the centre. They hid in people's yards and used side streets to avoid drones.".

    In a recent development, she said two soldiers entered her property. They had not been wearing any identifying insignia but had been speaking Ukrainian, she said - a language that Lina described as "Bandera", a derogatory term for Ukrainians.

    "You're going to have to leave. Why are you still here?" Lina noted they had asked her.

    She noted one had pointed a machine gun at her as she had stood outside her house, while another had gone to see my grandparents. She told me she had feared for her life and then fled her house for the night.

    The following day, she told me she had returned to my grandparents' street to check on them.

    She had found the door to the house they had been staying in open, she stated, despite the freezing conditions.

    Industry observers note that with drones buzzing overhead, Lina stated she had not dared look inside, but had later heard from neighbours that my grandparents had been found dead. She believed it had been the Ukrainian soldiers who visited her house who had shot them.

    Another neighbour, who I will call Maria, described discovering their bodies - my grandmother in bed, covered in a blanket, and my grandfather lying on the floor in a pool of now-dried blood.

    Maria also believed Ukrainian soldiers had killed them - because, she said, that she too had felt threatened by Ukrainian troops at the time.

    "If they had seen me they would have killed me too.".

    Her theory was that my grandparents had irritated the troops in some way.

    In a recent development, "Your grandparents caught them in a bad mood because your grandfather was always asking to be evacuated. And [the soldiers] were, you know, high. They were taking drugs. So your grandparents got in their way," she told me.

    Most of the other people in the village I spoke to also believe Ukrainian soldiers killed them, though their testimony is not based on direct evidence.

    The newly introduced local mayor, appointed by the Russian occupiers when they finally took control of Dachne in February, said she had been present at my grandparents' burial the following month, and said half of my grandmother's skull was missing.

    These accounts of how they might have died in January 2025 were deeply disturbing, though no-one had witnessed their deaths and the information I was given could not be independently verified.

    The villagers I spoke to - now living in occupied territory - did say there had been some tensions between themselves and Ukrainian troops at the time, because the soldiers had viewed those who remained in Dachne as supporters of Russia.

    The clinical causes of my grandparents' deaths are unclear.

    Their bodies were not exhumed for nearly 20 months, when the local authorities sent them to a morgue in the occupied region, where a basic autopsy was carried out by a forensics expert.

    He told me that my grandmother had died of an explosives injury to the skull - but could not specify its cause.

    As for my grandfather, it mentioned his body had shown no obvious signs of injury.

    I compared two satellite images of the house in which their bodies were found - from just before and just after when they are believed to have died - and could detect no significant damage to the building in the second image.

    I also spoke to a villager who said he had buried my grandparents.

    He noted he did not know anything about who killed them.

    According to recent reports, "I wasn't there. But why would you kill old people?" he asked.

    Anastasiya does not know if she will ever be able to give her grandparents (pictured) a dignified burial.

    Sources indicate that I examined military maps from DeepStateMap.Live, an open-source Ukrainian resource, and US think tank Institute for the Study of War. They suggested Ukrainian forces still held the street where my grandparents lived during the week they had died, although the front line had been shifting rapidly.

    My colleagues helped me identify the Russian military units that went on to capture Dachne. We found telephone numbers of Russian soldiers. But none of them agreed to speak to me.

    I turned to the Ukrainian military.

    A soldier from the 33rd Mechanised Brigade, who gave his name simply as Vlad, said his unit had still been in Dachne at the time my grandparents were believed to have died and that the Russians had been swiftly advancing.

    Another Ukrainian soldier I spoke to also confirmed Ukraine's troops had still been in control of some parts of Dachne in late January.

    We put our findings on the deaths of my grandparents to the Ukrainian military.

    Sources indicate that it mentioned it had no verified evidence on how they died, or which implicated its servicemen during the "intense hostilities". It added that investigating allegations of wrongdoing was the role of law enforcement.

    We also approached Russia's ministry of defence and Russia's embassy in London for comment - they did not respond.

    Sisters Sasha (right) and Anastasiya were reunited at Belgrade Airport.

    The Donetsk regional prosecutor's office, which is now based outside Russian-controlled territory, has documented alleged Russian war crimes reported by eyewitnesses in villages around Dachne during December 2024 and January 2025 - including the killing of five civilians in a basement in the nearby village of Kostyantynopilske.

    However, Ukrainian investigators have no equivalent cases registered in Dachne during that period. They have documented only three deaths there. My father and grandparents are not among them.

    Their bodies lie in occupied territory, and I do not know if I will ever be able to say goodbye properly and bury them with dignity.

    There is little more I can do for them, except one thing - mend my relationship with my sister and my mother.

    Almost three years after I last saw my sister, I fly to Belgrade where she now lives.

    Anastasiya (left) and her sister Sasha look through photos of their father.

    She is waiting for me at the airport, holding lilies, and a plate with a silly nickname on it that she gave me when we were children. We hug, cry and laugh. It feels as if something between us is finally falling back into place.

    At her flat, we look through family photographs and talk about my investigation and what I was able to find. My grief is still there, but it hurts a little less. I'm no longer carrying it alone.

    "Are you ready?" Sasha asks. She rings our mother - who has also moved to Serbia - and puts the phone on speaker.

    According to recent reports, "Hi, Mum. It's Nastya," I say. First there is silence. Then I hear her crying. "Nastya, my darling, hello," she replies.
